transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Priya Desai (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Redwood SRE), Carlos Nguyen (Redwood Product), Noah Kim (Helix Lead ML Eng), Aisha Patel (Helix Platform), Daniel Voss (Helix CTO)

Optional auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Summary: deep dive on how to get token-level telemetry into Helix's observability stack using OpenTelemetry, tradeoffs of sampling at span vs token level, how KV cache + batching opticalz (sic) affect token-level metrics, and pragmatic dashboards + alerts for SLO debugging. Agreed next steps: send OTLP config, run KV-cache microbenchmarks, schedule pilot kickoff.
Topics: OpenTelemetry token metrics, span sampling strategies, KV cache cold vs warm latency, batching and quantization effects, VPC/on-prem observability, Grafana dashboards and trace linking.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
[00:00] Priya (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for making time. quick intros then we'll dive into token-span sampling and how to map it into dashboards.
[00:12] Noah (Helix): hey thanks, we—big reason we're here is we've seen intermittent p99 spikes related to long-seqs, want to connect traces to tokens to root-cause.
[00:22] Ethan (Redwood SE): great, yeah we were sent the sample traffic profile earlier — long tail of seq lengths to 4k tokens, median around 360. that distribution matters for batching and the KV cache effectiveness.
[00:38] Aisha (Helix): just to be clear, priority is reproducible SLO debugging: when p99 > 600ms we need to know if it's batching, kv cache miss, or quantization fallback.
[00:51] Marta (Redwood SRE): noted. we usually instrument three surfaces: request span, model-inference span (per-request), and token spans (optional). token spans are higher cardinality — cost and storage tradeoffs.
[01:05] Daniel (Helix CTO): quick Q — can we keep token spans in our VPC/on-prem deployment only? don't want them leaving our network.
[01:12] Priya (Redwood): yes, for Private deployments all telemetry can go to customer-managed OTLP endpoint; we support OTLP over GRPC to local collectors, and you control retention.
[01:22] Ethan: couple of framing points before we deep-dive: 1) full token-level tracing is the richest signal but expensive; 2) span-sampling and token-sampling can reduce cost; 3) aggregations + token-anchored metrics let you get the best of both worlds.
[01:35] Noah: when you say token-anchored metrics, is that per-token latency buckets? we want to correlate model KV cache hits with tokens that miss.
[01:42] Ethan: right — emit a token metric like redwood.token.kv_hit with labels {model, shard, request_id, token_index, prefix_len_bucket}. then aggregate in Prometheus or store raw OTLP logs in Tempo/Jaeger.
[01:58] [small crosstalk] Noah: okay but prometheus cardinality concerns...
[02:05] Marta: exactly, prometheus high-cardinality is bad. we recommend two layers: 1) low-cardinality counters at request level (kv_hit_rate per prefix_bucket), 2) sampled token spans forwarded to tracing backend for deep dive.
[02:19] Priya: to add, we ship a Prometheus exporter in the runtime that emits tokenized summaries (token_histograms, cache_miss_ratio by prefix bucket) plus an OTLP exporter for traces.
[02:31] Aisha: what's default sampling we should start with? 1% token sampling? 10%?
[02:36] Ethan: typical starting point is request-level full spans always, token spans sampled at 0.5-2% globally. then bias-sample requests that exceed p95 latency or have unusual seq-lengths — so you get more samples in the tail.
[02:49] Noah: bias sampling sounds great. can we do a rule like sample all requests where p99 > 500ms or seq_len > 1024?
[02:56] Ethan: yep, we support policy-based sampling at the routing/config layer — you can punt to exporters only for those rules. we also support local reservoir sampling to avoid bursts.
[03:07] Daniel: on the KV cache side, what's the instrumentation we should expect? simple counters or per-key timing?
[03:14] Marta: runtime emits KV cache hit/miss counters and per-key latency histograms; but per-key labels are high cardinality so we use hashed buckets and prefix-length buckets. the exported span includes a small KV diagnostics map when a miss occurs.
[03:28] Aisha: is that map safe to send outside our VPC? it may contain model shard ids and partial key fingerprints.
[03:35] Priya: by default we redact sensitive IDs; customers can configure to include more detail inside a private collector. in on-prem we can send full diagnostics to your internal Tempo instance.
[03:44] Noah: useful. switching topics: batching — continuous batching affects p95/p99 differently than max-batch throughput, can we see per-batch metrics?
[03:53] Ethan: yes, the runtime emits batch_size, batch_wait_ms, batch_process_ms as request attributes. link those to token spans so you can see token-level latency contributions from queuing vs compute.
[04:06] [00:04:06] Noah: there's a mis-transcription — you said batch_process_ms?
[04:09] Ethan: batch_process_ms, yes. sorry.
[04:11] Noah: ok. also curious about quantization fallback events — sometimes we fall back to full FP for a shard and see latency jump.
[04:18] Marta: we emit a model_variant label and a quantization_flag at span-level. quantization-fallbacks are flagged as warnings and we recommend alerting on sudden increase in non-quantized requests.
[04:29] Aisha: can we have alerts: "quant-fallback rate > 1% in last 5m"?
[04:33] Priya: absolutely. standard dashboard templates include that panel. we'll share a Grafana JSON.
[04:39] [04:40] Noah: walkthrough request — show us the Grafana dashboard layout and how to drill from p99 to specific token spans.
[04:47] Ethan: demo time — I'm going to share a sample dashboard flow. (screen share noises, not transcribed)
[05:15] Ethan: top left: p50/p95/p99 by model + region. below that a heatmap of seq-length vs latency. click a spike in p99 and the trace panel narrows to sampled token spans; the trace shows token_index timings and KV cache hit flags inline.
[05:33] Daniel: that trace view — which tracing backend? Tempo? Jaeger?
[05:36] Ethan: we support Tempo, Jaeger, and commercial backends. for Private deployments we see a lot of customers use Tempo + Loki for logs and Prometheus for metrics.
[05:46] Noah: wanted to flag something: we use Lightstep internally and they'd like to ingest token spans too — any known issues?
[05:52] Priya: Lightstep works but cost model similar to other traces; if you plan high token-span retention we recommend sampling + upload raw OTLP to object storage for ad-hoc re-ingest.
[06:04] Aisha: what about storage for traces? we can't keep all token spans for 90 days.
[06:09] Marta: common pattern: keep request-level traces for 90d and token spans for 7-14d. keep metrics aggregated long-term (90d+).
[06:19] Noah: curious about correlating with application logs — do you emit a request_id header that we can propagate?
[06:24] Ethan: yes, the runtime sets redwood.request_id and we recommend passing that down into upstream logs. the token spans include request_id and token_index.
[06:35] [06:35] Ethan: small note on cardinality control: instead of token_index label you can export token_index_bucket (e.g., 0-7, 8-31, 32-127) which keeps useful shape without unbounded cardinality.
[06:47] Aisha: that would be fine. can we also see kv_cache_miss_reason? sometimes misses are due to eviction pressure vs cold start vs shard miss.
[06:55] Marta: yes we have miss_reason with enumerated values: eviction, cold_start, shard_mismatch, hash_error. those are low-cardinality.
[07:05] Noah: switching to sampling implementation: is sampling done in runtime or in the collector?
[07:09] Ethan: both options. runtime-level sampling reduces outbound bandwidth; collector-level sampling (e.g., OTEL collector) allows you to change rules without redeploying runtime but costs network. for Private you can keep runtime sampling conservative and rely on collector to expand in dev.
[07:24] Daniel: on-prem constraints — we need certs, mutual TLS to our OTLP endpoint, and HSM-backed keys.
[07:30] Priya: we support mTLS and can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for signing. will include config snippet.
[07:37] Noah: any example of policy rule you'd recommend?
[07:41] Ethan: rule example: sample tokens at 1% globally; if request p95 > 300ms OR seq_len > 1024 OR kv_miss_rate > 0.15 then sample token spans at 20% for that request. plus sample 100% of requests that hit explicit error codes.
[07:54] Aisha: is there a safe default for Prometheus exporter cardinality?
[07:58] Marta: keep label set small: model, region, prefix_len_bucket, cache_bucket. avoid request_id/token_index in Prometheus. use tracing backend for high-cardinality drilldowns.
[08:09] [08:09] Noah: question about real-time alerting: can token-level signals be used for on-call alerts or just for post-mortem?
[08:16] Ethan: both. you build low-cardinality rollups for alerting (e.g., kv_miss_rate by model) and use token spans to debug after alert fires. token spans are too noisy as primary alert signals.
[08:28] Daniel: latency budget conversation — for us, p99 target is 600ms. show me examples where batching saved cost but increased p99.
[08:36] Ethan: yes, we have panels that break down p99 into: queuing (batch_wait_ms), compute (batch_process_ms), kv_miss penalty, and network. quantization fallback adds compute penalty per-token.
[08:47] Noah: can we instrument quantization-fallback to correlate with certain inputs/prefixes?
[08:52] Marta: we include a small hashed fingerprint of the prompt prefix (non-reversible) as a label to find repeated patterns without exposing content.
[08:59] Aisha: excellent. now operationally, if we run a private deployment how do we upgrade runtime with new OTLP exporter without downtime?
[09:06] Priya: rolling upgrade; runtime supports hot restarts for the exporter config. for Dedicated/Private we can route a small percentage of traffic to the new runtime version, validate telemetry, then flip.
[09:18] Ethan: we also support canary tracing where traces from canary are marked and filtered.
[09:23] [09:23] Noah: can you share sample dashboards now?
[09:26] Priya: yes, we'll attach the Grafana JSON and a walkthrough doc after call.
[09:31] Daniel: a sticky point — cost. Token spans plus high-sample tracing may hit budget. what are options to quantify cost before we commit?
[09:39] Ethan: couple of ways: 1) run a short 24-72h microbenchmark with sampling enabled and measure OTLP egress and trace ingest volume; 2) use our cost-estimator (we'll share spreadsheet) that maps token-span sample rate to estimated storage and ingestion costs for common backends.
[09:56] Noah: let's do the microbenchmark. Aisha will send traffic profile.
[10:00] Aisha: yes will do. any recommended load profile shape?
[10:04] Ethan: send 7-day bucketed profile (p50/p95/p99, seq_len buckets) and we'll build a synthetic driver to replay it at low rate.
[10:11] [10:11] Marta: minor transcribe glitch: 'replay it at low rate' meant 'replay at production-like concurrency but limited time window'.
[10:18] Priya: closing recap: we'll share OTLP + prometheus config, Grafana JSON, cost estimator, and Ethan will own the KV microbench.
[10:26] Noah: thanks — this is helpful.
[10:29] Daniel: quick legal/security note — we will need SOC2 artifacts and a network diagram for the private deployment.
[10:35] Priya: we'll include SOC2 summary in the security pack.
[10:39] Aisha: last question — can Redwood's runtime emit token-level metrics into our existing Datadog instead of Prometheus?
[10:44] Ethan: yes we have an exporter for Datadog (statsd/OTLP). Datadog retention/cost model is similar, so sampling guidance applies.
[10:51] Noah: perfect.

End of transcript.
